title: creative wealth is wealth
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

today, I'm explicitly naming the paradigm shift that changed everything for me -- the belief that my creative energy is the source of my material abundance. my creativity is not a liability, a luxury, or a burden; it is my greatest resource.

I'll be naming the wound -- I'll share the story of working through shame, exile, and the long, lonely journey of risking everything for a vision. I'll tell you how I came to the idea of "the artist entrepreneur," how I realized that my artist child needed to grow up, and hold the chariot reins of my life. we'll explore 4 forms of abundance -- inner,d art, web worlds, and money -- and how they feed into each other.

in previous episodes, I've talked a lot about integrating art and business, or solving the puzzle of making money as a creative person in the world. I've come up with many solutions, but today I want to explicitly name the paradigm shift underneath all of the solutions, which fundamentally fuels my work and shapes the way that I exist in the world. I think all meaningful change starts from beliefs work.

this is something that I've articulated in my post, "the way of the artist entrepreneur" — that creative energy is the source of material abundance, that creative wealth is wealth in the material world. the intangible, immaterial, formless, imaginative, intuitive, sensed worlds is as every bit a valuable resource as the things in this world that we can touch, which feeds our bodies. this way of seeing the world is believing that our visions, ideas, feelings, perspectives, passions, is as every bit, if not more valuable than a pile of cash. because you can spend a pile of cash — it's gone. money is a finite resource. but if you spend your visions, ideas, passions, those ideas just create more ideas. those resources are generative and infinite.

and the problem for most of us, for me for many years, was the tension of this transformation — the bridge between the imagined, immaterial worlds into the real, shared, tangible world. part of it is because we live in a world that constantly diminishes and disempowers creative energy, or compartmentalizes creativity as something impractical and unrealistic. and then when we try to make money, when we try to sell something, there's a lot of internal resistance about money and marketing and sales. part of that has to do with frameworks and language, which is something I discussed in the last episode, "business words I never use."

in today's episode, I want to share with you my journey of integrating art and business — how I've come to this point of teaching what it is that I most needed to learn from my own wounds around this problem, and deconstruct some solutions to this challenge, namely the approaches of monetization and compartmentalization. I want to explore how this fundamental paradigm shift of integration between art and business was the secret key that unlocked everything for me. and then I will explore the four different forms of abundance: inner abundance, art abundance, web world abundance, and material abundance.

I am recording this episode right before starting to teach my business course, Digital Abundance, which will run live this month. when I wrote the invitations page, I did it in two sittings. it felt like bleeding from my bones. it felt so visceral in my body.

teaching as the hermit

as an artist and a guide, I've related a lot to the archetype of the hermit — that I've learned everything that I teach through hard, lonely experiences, mostly through nonstop journaling and processing and thinking and talking to the void for many years, because most business advice that other people gave me just never really worked. the most support that I've gotten was from esoteric systems of human design, gene keys, astrology, whereas well-intentioned friends who would give me ideas or suggestions — they don't live in my body, in my creative body. so what worked for them never worked for me.

I think at the beginning of starting a business, you think that there is a right way, a set of steps that you have to do to make it successful. but having a business is not like making a machine that works. it's not like buying a cookie cutter house. your business needs to work for your body. a business is organic, it's fluid and amorphous as you are, as life is. and so no one can tell you what to do. you can only learn to create it, inhabit it, and live it through ongoing experimentation.

whenever I teach something, a new course, I think of teaching as like leading an expedition — because I only teach topics that feel alive, electric, and with a bit of an edge of the unknown. I find whatever is there on the frontier of my obsessions, something that I've integrated or thought about for a long time, and that I lead a group to discover it, to adventure together. and after I teach that thing, that topic, the experience of teaching itself always catapults me to the next dimension. that's how I know I'm ready. I always teach what I'm ready to expand.

Digital Abundance is the last foundational course of my ecosystem. it's like the spinal cord of my body of meta work about being an artist on the internet. and you know how they say that you teach what you most need to learn, or in astrological terms, from Chiron, the wounded healer? well, this class is very much teaching from my wounds. and I think that when we create offerings, when we create work from the work of the wounds, that is where the greatest creative power — where all the juice lives.

the wound

so before I can tell you about this paradigm shift of why creative abundance is material abundance, let me talk about the wound. let me talk about the opposite of this belief. I know I'm not alone in feeling this.

the wound is the belief that the creative self, our creative selves, is a liability, a luxury, or an inconvenient burden — like a spoiled child that you have to take care of.

in my context, I was raised in a Chinese American immigrant family culture, where the cultural programming was to be a good, obedient Asian daughter — to do well in school, to go to an elite university, to get a high paying job, to have job stability, and make everyone proud. at the very least, don't make your family ashamed of you. and while I loved art and music since I was a young child, I was encouraged to become an engineer or a doctor and do some paintings as a hobby in my free time.

the underlying message was: let responsible adults do the adult things, and let my creativity be this invalid, this sensitive, somewhat sickly child who dreams in bed and can't really do anything in the harshness of the real world. in other words, that creative energy has no place in the material world, and choosing to be an artist might as well be choosing to starve, to choosing to be poor. and what does being poor mean in a capitalist society to immigrant parents? well, it means being lower status, which means bringing shame to your family, which means being a burden on them.

and if I were to peel back the shadow layers of this — as a child, I think I believed that how well I did in school or my accomplishments directly related to how worthy I was of attention, of love. and then as an adult, rather than accomplishments, the variable changed into money. how much money I made was equivalent to my worthiness of being loved.

my wound is that I used to be this overachieving, ambitious, hustler, Ivy League graduate that my parents were proud of. I tried to do something legible that felt like a compromise in my early twenties. I took internships in advertising, in architecture, in publishing. I worked in graphic design studios. I was a creative hustler for hire.

and then when I finally shed all the layers of skin and realized that at my core I was an artist — which I wrote about in a post in 2019 called "the art of finding my path" — what it did was veer me off the paved path completely. and it made me feel like I had betrayed my family. like I caused them shame and embarrassment. I was a burden. my mother would tell me that when other Chinese aunties asked her at dinner tables what her Columbia University graduate daughter was doing with her life, she didn't know what to say. she changed the subject.

those were my darkest years. I barely spoke to my family at all. every conversation with my mother ended in tears. I felt like an exile, walking alone towards what felt like my true destiny. and in this narrative, I'm the hero, answering a call to adventure. I knew that I was born for this, even if I hadn't figured out what this is. and I know this sounds really dramatic, but I'm not even joking. it is dramatic because it is how I felt.

so after 10 years of living in New York City, I left in 2020 to travel around the world and live nomadically. and then I came back after the pandemic to stay with my friends and noticed how everybody had promotions at their corporate jobs. my friends had these shiny household appliances. my brother, who's five years younger, had shiny household appliances. they had stock options. they had investment accounts.

and what did I have at age 29? I had a bank account with just enough to get by. I had parents who worried about me constantly. I had deep feelings that made me feel like I was constantly drowning in them. and I had a couple of years of life and travel experiences and an emerging body of creative work that I was trying to make sense of.

it took me so many years to see that what I had — even though it was illegible, immaterial, intangible to the constructs of our society — what I had was as worthy, if not more worthy, than shiny household appliances or investment accounts. because I was playing the very, very long game. I was risking my life on a big gamble that if I gave my creativity everything I had, I would be rewarded at the end. and this reward may not come in the form of cold, hard cash, but my life would reward me.

because my deep creative resources felt like an underwater treasure trove. it was full of jewels and gems and precious metals and mountains of gold. I just didn't know how to bring them up to the surface. I didn't know how to channel them. I didn't know how to share them. I didn't know how to make these treasures feed me in my day-to-day life or to create the material stability and abundance that I realized I actually wanted. but now, five years later, I do. and that is what teaching Digital Abundance is all about.

solutions that didn't work for me

so let me tell you about the solutions that did not work for me. if the problem puzzle is how do I make money as a creative artist person in a capitalist world, there are two common solutions — and a third one that I won't get into about getting money from funding or grants or fellowships. the two I'll talk about here are monetization and compartmentalization.

monetization

you probably know if you've followed my work that I hate the word monetize. I did not figure out how to monetize my passion. in fact, I wrote in the invitations page to Digital Abundance that this word monetize is forbidden — and I'm only half joking here. because monetization is too mechanistic, simplistic, linear, and too basic, honestly, of a term that completely skips the energy and essence of what we're working with.

let me give you two reasons.

reason one is that monetization, the paradigm of it, kills the creative passion and aliveness. it's less about what you do or the offerings that you make specifically, and more about the way in which you do them. sometimes if you make and sell your art, it creates commercial pressure on the art. there's a tension between what I think will sell consistently and what I truly deeply desire to make. if you have commercial pressure, it makes it hard to create from a place of genuine desire or risk-taking. and just the act of monetization feels like it's taking something alive, organic, and therefore fluid and unpredictable — and seeing how much money I can squeeze from it. it's imposing a capitalist mechanistic model on something that is inherently alive and wild. and let me reiterate — it is not what you do. it is not making money from your art. it is more about the mental model with which you approach it.

reason number two is that this paradigm creates long-term unsustainability. because when you look at something trying to monetize it, the design challenge here is to optimize for cash. it's not about your energy, it's not about what you desire, it's not about your intuition — it's about money. so the end justifies the means under this paradigm. and I think that's unsustainable in the long term because when you try to make a machine that can take care of you, maybe you'll feel relieved at the beginning, but over time this machine will break down. the fuel that sustains it — your passion, your ideas, your inspiration — will slowly, in my experience, be eroded by the paradigm and mental model of monetization. in other words, I get bored of myself. I get tired of doing the same things and it will kill my creativity very slowly.

compartmentalization

the second solution or paradigm is compartmentalization, and there are two ways that people do this.

the first option is getting a stable day job and then doing creative pursuits on the side, which definitely works for many people. there are many successful artists and writers, however you define success, who have done this. the way that I think about it is that working for yourself creates a certain kind of cognitive burden, a load on your nervous system. no one's telling you what to do. there is no steady paycheck. there's a lot of uncertainty. that can feel extremely difficult and ungrounding. so there's a compromise in every configuration. and maybe there are circumstances in your life that make that kind of risk untenable.

for me, I was in a situation in which the pain of staying at a job, even if it was part time, was greater than the pain of suffering as I tried to build my business. because every second I spent working for someone else's garden was a moment of my life that I would never get back. my body hated the feeling of my labor being valued and weighed and measured by another person. and I wanted to expand and create my own worth.

the second option is compartmentalization within your own business. an example of this is being a web designer for hire by day and an artist by night — which I have done. this is an easy, digestible identity split. again, it's less about what you do and more about how you navigate or inhabit those identities. in the early years of doing this work, I would have a lot of clients who were not totally aligned. and I kind of showed up to client work as a different person than how I showed up to my own creative practice. the problem is not having clients, but how I was recognized and seen — the ways in which I was able to bring my artistic self to that work.

it took me a long time to realize that even client work, even when someone else is paying you to be in collaborative process with them, it is not about the outcome — it is about everything you bring to the process. so if I was in a process with a client or a project that did not feel aligned, that did not allow me to bring my creativity and my artistic energy to it, it created this internal tension and this energetic drain that sucked the energy from everything that I was doing. it made me money, but it made me very tired.

it is possible to have a day job, to compartmentalize your client work in a way which allows you to feel whole and integrated. but I think the ways in which we do that needs to be done with care and attention.

I think our society wants easy, obvious ways of making money — like making money is just a series of buttons that you press, like an orange juice machine: insert orange into machine and juice comes out. but having a business is fluid. a business is like a home, a world, a garden. ultimately, my definition of having a business is simple. you're creating a living resource. that's it. when you ignore all the shoulds, at the center is a business as a living resource. you realize that there are infinite ways to create a living resource. you're not obligated to fit into a specific identity. you don't need to be digestible — because trying to digest yourself into one line, the question I would encourage you to ask is: digestible to who? are those people even the right people to metabolize your work?

the best, most strategic and efficient way to create a living resource is actually counterintuitive. it's not about creating something for someone else or what you think someone else needs. it's creating something that is so unique to you that it can only come from you, that is so aligned with you that it gives you energy. this creation, this resource, is generative both as a process and as an outcome.

what is possible beyond monetization or compartmentalization? integration. the integration of the creative self with every other part of your life.

the shift

and so the shift is that you realize your artist child does not need to be protected from responsibility. your artist child needs to grow into their power.

this shift happened for me when I started examining my complicated relationship with money. I read a lot of money books. I looked at my shadow beliefs, my wounds. and that year I said two important things out loud. saying things out loud for me is really important because I'm a self-projected projector.

so when I was working with an artist friend on their systems, I heard myself telling them — the work that I'm here to do is to make artists rich. and I was kind of embarrassed after I said that. like, really, I'm here to make artists rich? but it stayed with me.

and then maybe a few months later, I was walking my dog in the park and another woman with a dog asked me what I did. and I said, "I'm an artist entrepreneur." and that summer, right after that experience, I wrote "the way of the artist entrepreneur."

for many years, I saw my artist self as like this tender, sensitive, poetic inner child that I needed to protect from the harshness of the world. the paradigm was artist child, business adult. the slow shift — which happened over months, if not years — is realizing that she doesn't need my protection. she needs to grow up and grow into her power to hold the reins of the chariot that is my creative life.

and then I started asking myself: what if I allowed her a seat at the table? what if I gave her the reins? what if she was in the driver's seat — not my responsible, strategic, hustler self, but her? how would she lead if she was the leader? what if I trusted her — her wild imagination, her deep intuitive knowing — to be the leader of my business and my life?

and I know that will be hard. can I trust her with it when all the adults around her have disempowered her her entire life? can I feel safe with her?

this question was both a huge revelation and something that I had to allow to sink into me slowly over time — to feel in my body and practice when I have a decision I need to make, letting her take the lead. noticing when I'm operating from the thinking mind as opposed to the intuitive sensing body. noticing where she lives in my body.

it is through deep integration of this artist energy in my life that has been the underlying thread which connected so much of my work. I did a three episode mini-series — make the work, share the work; make an offering, weave the web; and make art the center of your world. this paradigm shift is at the heart of all of this.

because what does being an artist entrepreneur actually mean? it means that you use your creative energy to create living resources for yourself and for others. and that's all that business is — resources that other people can use, that other people give you their resources for. and what is the greatest resource of all? creative energy. imagining something into existence. the intuitive, the wild, the nonlinear, the felt, the sensed, the embodied — the things that AI could not and will not replace.

and the problem is that we're not taught how to do this. we're not taught how to use it. we're not taught to bridge the gap between underwater treasures and sustenance in the material earthly realms. instead, we monetize it and kill it, or we compartmentalize it, or we compromise or abandon it, or give it up entirely.

again, this is a process. perhaps integration feels too risky for you in this moment. there is no right solution for how to solve the puzzle of the ways in which your creative life fits in with your material life and need for money. we each find our own configurations of solutions. but I think this paradigm shift is important to name as one powerful possibility.

4 forms of abundance

let me tell you about how I see the four different types of abundance and how they feed each other. the name Digital Abundance came to me in early 2025 because of what it represented and encompassed — that inner abundance is channeled into the digital world through art and web worlds and becomes money, which is digital. for me, the digital world, the internet, is basically a connected consciousness. it's like the universe or a webbed collective mind of creations and thoughts. rather than putting money at the hierarchy of what is worthy and valuable in this world.

the first abundance, the primary form of abundance, is inner abundance. and that is your emotions, your sensitivity, your intuition, your inspirations, your thoughts, your perceptions, your perspectives, your experiences. all of that is abundance. all of that is raw material. at one time I said to a friend, I think I was crying at the time, I was like, "wow, I'm poor financially, but I'm rich in feelings." and that felt like a burden, but now I know that it's a gift. to be rich in feelings, to be rich in possibility and thoughts and desires is abundance.

the second form is art abundance. that when you make things, when you write things, when you digest your inner world into tangible art form, whether that's digital or physical, your creativity is an expression of your inner abundance that other people can relate to, can see, can touch, can feel. it's a resource for them. whatever you create in your art comes from the way in which you metabolize your life. and we're all just figuring out how to be alive here. so the art you create is a gift for the rest of us. it's witnessing a human being being in conversation with life. that is not something that AI can do. it is about sharing your way of seeing the world and grappling with the hardest questions that we don't have answers for. what does it mean to be alive, to love, to experience loss and fear and confusion? what does it mean to live knowing that we're going to die?

the third form of abundance is web worlds. in the digital age, we have a unique opportunity to show and share the abundance of our inner worlds, of our art through the internet. this is why I keep talking about the internet as the portal and vessel of creative power. because when you weave a digital world, you are offering abundance. it's generative. your world becomes this infinite resource that ripples out into places that you will never know. I wrote about this in a post called "why worldbuilding is wealthbuilding."

and the fourth type of abundance is money. unless you keep wads of cash under your bed, money is just a number on a screen. money is a number that makes you feel something. money is creative energy. money, like art worlds, like web worlds, is the manifestation, the symptom of being in flow — sharing your resources with others and receiving resources and nourishment in return. money is digital abundance and it comes from your digital abundance of your art and your web worlds, both of which come from your inner worlds.

so when it comes to growing a business, it is not about creating systems that can optimize for money in a consistent, stable way. it is about the dance and conversation between your inner worlds, your energy, the art you create, the web worlds you weave — into flowing and receiving resources. it is not about selling your art for money. it's about integrating the energy of your art, your creative work, into everything that you do, regardless of whether or not money is involved. this means breaking the wall between free art and paid work. because art is priceless, it has infinite value, art is a gift — and paid offerings could be an artful distillation of the same creative energy.

I think of a quote by the physicist Carl Sagan. he says, "the cosmos is within us. we are made of star stuff. we are a way for the universe to know itself." in other words, your business can be made from the same star stuff, the same material that makes your art. your effort to grow this business can feel effortless. your way of sharing and offering can be created from the energy of this star stuff.

this is what I've spent a decade learning and what I'm finally ready to lead an expedition on and teach.

closing

take care, until next time.
